newsitem.title: USA: Zedillo predicts Clinton visit will strengthen ties.
newsitem.headline: Zedillo predicts Clinton visit will strengthen ties.

text.p: Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, downplaying reports of tension in U.S.-Mexican ties, predicted on Monday President Bill Clinton's visit would reaffirm the strong relationship enjoyed by the two countries.

In an interview with U.S. public television, Zedillo also criticised the U.S. procedure of "certifying" the anti-narcotics efforts of other countries, saying the mechanism clearly had not proven effective.
The president said U.S. experience showed it was "not an effective means to face the drug trafficking problem."

Zedillo said the certification process contradicted the cooperative anti-narcotics efforts both countries were trying to encourage. "We do say, quite clearly, that the U.S. government, and especially the U.S. Congress, should reconsider this certification process," he said.

In an interview taped on Thursday and aired on Monday, the Mexican president said U.S.-Mexican ties were closer than ever before, in no small part because of Clinton's support of the North American Free Trade Agreement and his decision to help Mexico during the 1994 peso crisis.
"With President Clinton we have found respect -- and that is something we Mexicans value significantly," Zedillo told public television's "NewsHour with Jim Lehrer."
Clinton arrived in Mexico on Monday for his first presidential trip there. He is the first U.S. president to visit the Mexican capital since Jimmy Carter in 1979.

"I expect that this visit will reaffirm our friendship, our mutual respect, and that we will be able to make further progress on the specific issues that concern both countries, such as trade, drug trafficking, migration, border issues," the Mexican leader said.

Zedillo said Mexico had instituted changes to eliminate corruption among high-level Mexican drug agents and stressed his country's concern about new U.S. immigration laws cracking down on illegal immigrants.

"Our main point is that migrants -- whatever their condition, legal or illegal -- should be at all times treated as human beings. Their basic human rights should be respected: their labour rights should be respected," he said.

Zedillo also said the problem of migration would persist as long as there was a great economic disparity between the two North American neighbours, and the only effective solution was to increase Mexico's economic development.
"You can spend a lot of money in law enforcement but if these differences persist, there will always be an incentive to go around the law and migrate," he said.
